results.question: What do the screen-combat and fight-choreography books say about making a punch read as re
results.answer:
A punch reads as real when three things line up: the fake strike is aimed at the geometry of the camera, the impact is sold by camera and actor together, and everything runs on an **agreed timing** that the audience perceives as instant cause and effect [S14]. The books are unanimous that the illusion is cooperative — nobody actually gets hit, and credibility comes from choreography, camera, and performance rather than contact.

## Distance and strike geometry

The distance rules invert real fighting. In an over-the-shoulder shot the attacker punches almost at the target, aiming slightly to the camera side, but stays **out of distance** so the fist can never connect; in a profile two-shot the striker must be within reach but punch **offline** — to the side of the face, over the shoulder, at the imaginary parrot — because at a true 90-degree profile the miss is readable [S2]. A little angle fixes that, and once you're at a diagonal only the side nearer the camera line sells, so circling fights force constant shifts of both distance and angle [S2]. Camera distance and angle are ultimately artistic choices about how subjects fill the frame, but they must still convey enough information for the audience to read the action [S5] — which is why fights nearly always open in a long/full/wide shot that establishes relative size, surroundings, and how far out of reach the fighters begin [S9].

## Camera and the reaction

Camera angles must be chosen so fake hits read as actual connecting strikes; if the audience can't see what the actors are doing, the illusion breaks [S4]. Shot planning works hand-in-hand with choreography, so each change in angle or framing demands an adjustment in the choreography, and a cut on a move needs a different angle afterward or the join is jarring — shots should set each other up, showing the next threat before the hero sees it [S3]. The reaction is often put on the camera itself: a quick shudder on a big punch — flinching screen-right as a right haymaker lands — sells power and can even cover sloppy alignment to a degree, though the books warn not to go overboard [S1]. The receiving performance matters just as much: the screen fighter sells the fight through actions, facial expressions, and body language, holding the fight as genuinely real in their mind so the landings feel like a well-oiled machine [S6].

## The agreed timing beat

Film timing is "agreed timing": the person getting hit knows about the blow beforehand, and both actors cooperate to build the illusion — unlike a real fight, where timing shifts constantly like a live chess match [S14]. The response is locked to the contact: the camera flinch happens just as the hit lands, so the whole frame feels the punch [S1], and the recipient's body should commit into the strike with consistent contact points and a shared weight lean, with a deliberate release afterward [S7, S8]. Around that beat, believable sound effects and rhythm-heightening editing finish the job, on top of a believable cause and motivation for the fight itself [S13]. In practice this is a rehearsed dance repeated for coverage, demanding stamina, knowledge of every cue, and constant awareness of the camera [S6, S10].

One angle the sources don't analyze: none of the books examines from a perceptual or biomechanical standpoint *how* a body communicates force and intent to an observer. What they offer instead is craft — the actor's physical and facial commitment selling the moment [S6, S10], plus camera and sound doing the rest.
